critic_changes: Opened all four cited documents; every original quote was found verbatim on its page, and all titles and dates check out (IMF CR 26/212 dated July 10, 2026; WB 10th Economic Update dated AUGUST 2026; IMF PR dated April 3, 2015; the PFR excerpt has no printed date, so year-only 2025 is kept as the release year).

Arc sentence 2: 'as oil production began' changed to 'as oil production rose'. The PFR says the 2008–2019 boom was fed by rising oil production and the Jubilee field came online in 2011, not that production began in 2006.

Arc sentence 5: dropped 'helped by record gold prices and a cocoa rebound'. The cited World Bank passage ties gold and cocoa to the current account surplus, not to growth. It now says growth picked up 'while inflation fell and reserves were rebuilt', which the IMF report supports.
Arc sentence 4: reordered to 'an IMF program approved in 2023 and a debt restructuring'. The IMF report confirms the May 2023 approval.

Thread 'Oil and a borrowed boom': swapped the heading-style quote 'Starting in 2010...' for two PFR passages that support the text: expansionary fiscal policy and private credit fed by oil, and the Jubilee field set to come online in 2011. The text now says the field 'came online in 2011' (11.3 in 2011 is the series maximum), and 'rising public spending' now matches the source's 'expansionary fiscal policy'.

Thread 'Debt crisis and repair': dropped 'domestic and foreign' from the restructuring, since the cited passages don't specify it. Added an IMF staff-appraisal citation for the claim that inflation fell and reserves were rebuilt, which was unsupported before.

Thread 'Gold up, oil fading': removed 'Exports now lean on gold' and 'Recent growth has come mostly from services, farming and mining rather than oil'. No opened passage supports the farming/mining split. The text now says what the quotes say: gold and cocoa drove the external surplus in 2025, and oil output fell as fields matured.

Thread 'Few jobs, thin investment': added the World Bank passage on gains concentrated in gold and services with limited employment absorption, to support 'sectors that hire few people'. 'Cutting capital spending' became 'spending less than planned on capital projects' to match 'under-execution of capital expenditure'. Removed 'investment fell to 9.7 percent of GDP in 2024' from the thread because it repeats the tension and has no source behind its causal link.

since_last_year: 'gold drove a large export surplus' became 'record gold prices drove a large external surplus', since the source refers to the current account. 'Closed its lending program' became 'completed its lending program', to match the IMF's 'sixth and final review'.

Tension: the first claim now rests on an opened source. The IMF 2015 press release opens 'After two decades of strong and broadly inclusive growth', so the vague 'sources describe ... since the early 1990s' became 'In 2015 the IMF described two decades of strong growth'. Dropped 'as capital spending was cut' as a causal claim about the investment fall.

Number check: every growth figure (1.9, 5.3, 11.3, 2.3, 0.5, -0.2, 3.9, 4.0, 2.8, 4.2) and the 1971/2006 level claim match GHA.json. Flag for the orchestrator: the investment figures in the tension (9.7 in 2024, 27.0 in 2015) come from series NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS, but growth_problem.G6 gives 11.9 percent for 2024 for the same indicator, a different data vintage. If the page shows the G6 figure, readers will see two numbers for 2024 investment, and that needs reconciling in the data.
No banned phrases, no recommendation language. 3 distinct recent tier 1 sources (IMF 2026, World Bank 2026, World Bank 2025), so the story stays tier 1.

growth_story.headline: Ghana's income per person is at its highest yet, after an oil-era boom, a decade of slower growth and a 2022 debt crisis now largely behind it.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2005, income per person in Ghana grew a steady 1.9 percent a year, and only in 2006 did it pass its 1971 high. Growth then sped up to 5.3 percent a year in 2006–2013, peaking at 11.3 percent in 2011, as oil production rose and public spending and private credit expanded. From 2014 growth slowed to 2.3 percent a year: it fell to 0.5 percent in 2014 and -0.2 percent in 2015, when the IMF pointed to large budget and external deficits and acute power shortages. A recovery in 2017–2019 gave way to the pandemic and then a debt crisis in 2022, which led to an IMF program approved in 2023 and a debt restructuring. Growth picked up to 3.9 percent in 2024 and 4.0 percent in 2025 while inflation fell and reserves were rebuilt, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025. Over 2016–2025 it averaged 2.8 percent a year, down from 4.2 percent in 2006–2015.

threads.title: Oil and a borrowed boom
threads.text: From 2008, public spending and private credit expanded on the hope of oil money, and the Jubilee oil field came online in 2011, the year income per person grew fastest. The World Bank says the boom was partly carried by growing budget and external deficits, which built up debt.

growth_story.tension: In 2015 the IMF described two decades of strong growth, but income per person rose only 1.9 percent a year in 1990–2005, as fast population growth absorbed much of the gain in total output. And while the sources describe a strong recovery, investment fell to 9.7 percent of GDP in 2024, from 27.0 percent in 2015.
